data.title: Chickenpox (varicella) — viva
data.summary: Viral infections · 15 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Chickenpox (varicella)** (Viral infections)_

**Q1. What is chickenpox? Agent and transmission?**
- Primary infection with varicella-zoster virus (HHV-3, alpha-herpesvirus)
- Spread by respiratory droplets/aerosols and direct contact with vesicle fluid; highly contagious (secondary attack rate ~90% in susceptible household contacts)
- Incubation 10–21 days (average 14–16); infectious from 1–2 days before rash until all lesions are crusted (~5–7 days)

**Q2. Describe the pathogenesis.**
- Inhalation → replication in the respiratory tract and regional nodes → primary viraemia → liver/spleen → secondary viraemia → skin (in waves → crops)
- Virus then remains latent in dorsal root and cranial nerve ganglia → may reactivate later as herpes zoster

**Q3. Describe the rash.**
- Mild prodrome (fever, malaise) in adults, often none in children
- Itchy rash starts on the scalp/face and trunk (centripetal distribution) and spreads to limbs; mucosae may have erosions
- Evolution: macule → papule → vesicle ('dewdrop on a rose petal') → pustule → crust within 24 h; lesions in all stages at the same time (pleomorphism) due to crops over 3–5 days
- Heals in 1–2 weeks; may leave scars (especially if scratched/infected)

**Q4. Differentiate chickenpox from smallpox.**
- Chickenpox: centripetal, superficial thin-walled vesicles, lesions in different stages, mild fever, palms/soles spared, no prodromal severe toxaemia
- Smallpox: centrifugal (face and extremities incl. palms/soles), deep-seated firm vesicles/pustules, all lesions at same stage, severe prodrome; now eradicated (1980)

**Q5. Other differentials?**
- Disseminated herpes simplex or zoster, eczema herpeticum, hand-foot-mouth disease (coxsackie — palms, soles, mouth), insect bite reactions/papular urticaria, PLEVA, impetigo, scabies with pyoderma, drug eruptions (AGEP), rickettsial pox, mpox

**Q6. What are the complications?**
- Commonest in children: secondary bacterial infection (S. aureus, group A strep — cellulitis, necrotising fasciitis, toxic shock)
- Pneumonia (commonest serious complication in adults, smokers and pregnant women)
- CNS: acute cerebellar ataxia (children), encephalitis, Reye's syndrome (with aspirin — avoid aspirin), Guillain–Barré
- Haemorrhagic varicella (purpura fulminans), hepatitis, myocarditis, nephritis, arthritis, thrombocytopenia
- Immunocompromised: progressive disseminated varicella with high mortality

**Q7. Discuss varicella in pregnancy.**
- Mother: higher risk of severe varicella pneumonia
- Congenital (fetal) varicella syndrome — infection in the first 20 weeks (risk ~1–2%): cicatricial skin scars in dermatomal distribution, limb hypoplasia, eye defects (chorioretinitis, cataract), microcephaly, low birth weight
- Neonatal varicella: mother develops rash 5 days before to 2 days after delivery → severe disease in baby (no maternal antibodies) — give VZIG to the baby and acyclovir if disease develops
- Exposure of non-immune pregnant woman: VZIG within 10 days; acyclovir if rash develops

**Q8. How will you investigate?**
- Clinical diagnosis usually
- Tzanck smear (multinucleated giant cells — not specific)
- PCR of vesicle fluid (best), DFA; serology IgM/IgG (immunity status)
- CBC, LFT, chest X-ray if pneumonia suspected

**Q9. Treatment of chickenpox.**
- Healthy children: symptomatic — calamine lotion, oral antihistamines, paracetamol (no aspirin — Reye's), trimmed nails, hygiene
- Oral acyclovir 20 mg/kg (max 800 mg) four times daily for 5 days if started within 24 h — for adolescents >12 y, adults, chronic skin/lung disease, on steroids, secondary household cases
- Adults: acyclovir 800 mg five times a day for 7 days or valacyclovir 1 g thrice daily for 7 days
- IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 h for immunocompromised, pneumonia, encephalitis, pregnancy with complications

**Q10. What is the varicella vaccine?**
- Live attenuated Oka strain
- IAP schedule (India): 2 doses — 15 months and 4–6 years (catch-up: 2 doses ≥3 months apart in children <13 y, 4 weeks apart ≥13 y); not in the national (UIP) schedule
- Contraindicated in pregnancy and severe immunosuppression; avoid pregnancy for 1 month after
- Post-exposure: vaccine within 3–5 days; VZIG (within 10 days) for immunocompromised, pregnant non-immune, neonates

**Q11. What is breakthrough varicella?**
- Varicella >42 days after vaccination — mild, few lesions (often <50), mostly papular rather than vesicular, low fever — still contagious

**Q12. Discuss the isolation advice.**
- Exclude from school/work until all lesions crust (about 5–7 days after onset)
- Hospital: airborne and contact precautions; non-immune health workers exposed should avoid patient contact from day 8 to day 21 after exposure

**Q13. Why are adults sicker than children?**
- More vigorous immune (cell-mediated) response and more pneumonia; smoking and pregnancy increase risk

**Q14. What is the link between varicella and zoster?**
- Same virus — chickenpox is primary infection; zoster is reactivation of latent VZV in a sensory ganglion when cell-mediated immunity falls (age, HIV, malignancy)
- Zoster lesions can transmit chickenpox (not zoster) to non-immune contacts

**Q15. What is Ramsay Hunt syndrome? (often linked question)**
- Zoster of the geniculate ganglion — ipsilateral facial palsy + ear pain + vesicles in the ear canal/pinna ± anterior-tongue taste loss, tinnitus, vertigo
- Treat with antivirals and steroids early

## Quick spotter facts
- Lesions in all stages at once, centripetal — chickenpox
- 'Dewdrop on a rose petal' vesicle
- Avoid aspirin — Reye's syndrome

## Note
Vaccine schedule follows IAP recommendations; confirm the current IAP schedule before use.

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Viral infections); national immunisation guidance (IAP). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
